newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - HK Christians trust in God for handover.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK Christians trust in God for handover.

text.p: Leaders around the world have warned they will be watching when China takes back control of Hong Kong at midnight on June 30.
Hong Kong Christians hope God will be looking on too.

While faith is a constant comfort to many of the more than half a million Christians in the territory, many are anxious about its return to the embrace of a motherland ruled by an atheist Communist Party.
"Deep down in their hearts, I think a lot of Christians are worried," said a Protestant pastor who, like many of those doubtful about the church's future, declined to be identified.
Many Hong Kong Christians fled communist China or are the children of exiles, making them all too aware of the decades- long suffering of their religious brethren on the mainland, he said.

During the ultra-leftist chaos of late Chairman Mao Zedong's 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution, Christians were targeted by youthful Red Guards as followers of a reactionary foreign creed. Churches were closed and clergy were thrown into labour camps.
"The past experience is a kind of pyschological scar," said the pastor. "It's inevitable."
RELIGIOUS FREEDOM GUARANTEED
Hidden fears among Hong Kong's large and vigorous Christian community of a possible return to oppression may be common, but they are far from universal.

Almost two decades of reform in China have erased much of the leftist dogma of the past. While church organisations remain tightly controlled, a large degree of freedom of worship has been restored to Christians, Buddhists and Moslems.

Even more importantly, Beijing has enshrined its promise not to change religious life in the Basic Law, China's constitution for post-colonial Hong Kong, said Tso Man-king, general secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council.
"There should be no concern at all. Religious freedoms are fully guaranteed in the Basic Law," Tso told Reuters. "I don't think they will be eroded."
Also bolstering confidence among many Christians is the knowledge that the eyes of the world will be on Hong Kong and its 6.4 million residents in the years after the handover.

Pope John Paul has said he will be watching closely and Washington and other Western governments have vowed to monitor developments in the territory, which was wrested from China by British gunboat diplomacy in the mid-19th century.
Chinese officials have left no doubt they will not interfere in Hong Kong's religious life, and it was clearly not in their interests to change that approach, Tso added.
"It would be very expensive to interfere in religious freedom ... also they understand the church is not an anti-revolutionary body," he said.
PRIVATE WORRIES, PUBLIC CONFIDENCE

Such confidence is publicly echoed by Hong Kong's Catholic Church, which ministers to a flock of almost 250,000 and dismisses suggestions it has already taken action to counter possible government interference in the years ahead.

Sino-Vatican ties have long been strained by China's refusal to allow its state-controlled Catholic Patriotic Association to acknowledge papal leadership, forcing many Catholics to risk detention by worshiping in secret.
Last year the Pope appointed Shanghai-born Monsignor Joseph Zen as co-adjudicator bishop of Hong Kong, which means he will eventually succeed Cardinal Joseph Wu as Catholic leader.
By appointing a bishop with right of accession before the handover, the Pope effectively bypassed any need to consult with Beijing on the issue after July 1.

But Mary Seung of the Catholic Social Communications Office, the church's public voice in Hong Kong, said reports that the appointment had been made to ensure China had no role in future clergy selection were mistaken.

A recent reorganisation of the diocese to create smaller communities of believers was a move to improve parishioners' religious life -- and not an attempt to guard against future official interference, Seung said.
"We are optimistic, we are not worried," she added.
"Of course God is watching," she said with a laugh, when asked if the community expected a divine interest to be taken in post-handover Hong Kong.
DIFFERING DEFINITIONS

While established church groups were unlikely to come under serious pressure after the handover, more evangelical or socially active churches could raise Beijing's ire, said one leading Catholic activist.

Both the Catholic church in China and the official Three-Self Protestant organisation are banned from proselytising, seeking to convert people, or from expressing their faith through social action -- common forms of religious conduct in Hong Kong.
"The understanding of Christian activities in the eyes of the Chinese authorities is quite narrow," the activist said.
Moves by future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa to boost curbs on political groups could hit some churches, she added.
"We may fall into the category of political groups ... then we may be under the same threat," she said. "We feel very uncertain and very worried about the future."

Some of Hong Kong's smaller and less orthodox evangelical groups -- whose ranks include one sect that advises followers to drink hydrogen peroxide -- are frightened the territory's new leadership will be less than tolerant.
Despite such fears, one evangelist minister said many were looking forward to ever-closer ties to the mainland and its hundreds of millions of potential converts.

"We treat this kind of crisis as a kind of opportunity. Because of the handover, we will have more opportunities to evangelise in mainland China," he said. But he added that such activities could enrage Beijing if carried out too blatantly. "We will have to do it carefully," he said.
